title: Lesson 88: The Future of Agent Economies: Standards and Interoperability
description: Tests which protocol layer carries which kind of work, how a signed intent mandate authorizes an agent to spend, and the controls that keep a shared proxy credential and an opaque counterparty's artifact from becoming an incident.

questions.question: A platform team consolidates its internal tooling behind one MCP proxy that fronts five downstream systems with a single static client ID, allows clients to register dynamically, and runs no consent check of its own. Which statement best describes the exposure?
options: It is one credential holding five sets of permissions, and the blast radius belongs to whoever wrote the proxy
It removes the integration tax, because the four confused deputy conditions are all satisfied
It is safe once redirect URIs are validated by pattern matching instead of exact string comparison
It is safe once the third party sets its own consent cookie on the user's browser
questions.explanation: The lesson names the confused deputy attack as possible when a proxy uses a static client ID, registers clients dynamically, relies on a third-party consent cookie, and adds no per-client consent check. A proxy that fronts many systems with one credential is not many integrations, so the blast radius belongs to whoever wrote the proxy. The required control is per-client consent recorded per user and checked before the third-party authorization flow begins.

questions.question: A user delegates a purchase to an agent with instructions to buy tickets the moment they go on sale, subject to price limits and timing. What does the signed intent mandate do in the delegated, human-not-present flow?
options: It replaces the cart mandate with a single reusable authorization code
It records the user's instruction only after the purchase has already completed
It serves as verifiable pre-authorized proof that lets the agent generate a cart mandate on your behalf once those conditions are met
It requires the user to approve every cart in real time before payment can settle
questions.explanation: In the human-not-present flow the user signs a detailed intent mandate up front that specifies the rules of engagement, including price limits, timing and other conditions. That mandate is verifiable pre-authorized proof, which is what allows the agent to generate a cart mandate by itself once those conditions are met. The lesson notes the conditional clause is the difference between a delegation and a blank check.

questions.question: A warranty verdict arrives from a supplier's opaque agent and would trigger an automatic 400 dollar refund in the returns workflow. Which control does the lesson recommend?
options: Trust the verdict, because the counterparty's Agent Card declared the warranty claim skill
Provenance on the artifact, a threshold, and a named rule for what may be automated
Show the verdict to a person, because opacity means the result can never be validated
Request every skill the card advertises so the verdict can be independently re-derived
questions.explanation: The lesson treats an artifact from an opaque counterparty as untrusted input in the same way a web form is untrusted input. Provenance on the artifact, a threshold and a named rule for what may be automated is what keeps a verdict from firing an irreversible refund. Opacity is precisely why that step cannot be skipped, since the artifact is the only part of the exchange your system receives.
